summary: Standards-track Telnet option that lets a client tell the server where the user's X Window display is. That way, graphical programs started on the remote machine know where to show their windows.

plainLanguage.summary: The X Display Location option lets Telnet hosts exchange the location of the user's X display. One host asks for it, and the other replies with a text address.

subtitle: A Telnet option for requesting and sending the user's X display location.

tldr.problem: A remote Telnet host may need the client's X display location to start another X application for the user.
tldr.mechanism: After option negotiation, one side requests the location with SEND and the other returns it with IS as an NVT ASCII string.
tldr.outcome: The location is sent only in response to a request, and the option is off by default.

today: RFC 1096 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Share an X Display Location
sections.content: When a user runs a Telnet client under the X Window System, the remote Telnet host may need to know the client's display location. This lets the user start other X applications from the remote host using the same display. RFC 1096 defines a Telnet option for making that information available.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote computer may need the location of the screen where the user's X applications should appear. This option lets it request that location over Telnet.

sections.title: Negotiating and Requesting the Location
sections.content:
The option is named X-DISPLAY-LOCATION (XDISPLOC), with code 35. WILL and DO establish permission for later exchange; the default is WON'T and DON'T, so no location is exchanged. Once both hosts have exchanged WILL and DO, only the sender of DO may request the location.

The requester sends a SEND subcommand, and only the sender of WILL may return the location in an IS subcommand. The location must not be sent spontaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: The hosts first agree to exchange the information. Then the DO side asks for it, and the WILL side sends it in reply.

sections.title: The Display Location String
sections.content:
The value is an NVT ASCII string using the usual Unix DISPLAY form: <host>:<dispnum>[.<screennum>]. No extraneous characters, such as spaces, may be included. The example in the RFC returns SRI-NIC.ARPA:0.0.

A local display value may lack a host name, such as :0 or unix:0.0. The RFC says the Telnet client must modify such a value appropriately before sending it to the remote Telnet host.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply is a text value that names a host and display, with an optional screen number. The client may need to adjust a local value that has no host name.

references.text: Hedrick, C., "Telnet Terminal Speed Option", RFC 1079, December 1988.
